statements: Repeated guessing game; rounds t=1,...,T.
Adversary chooses y_t in[0,1] and keeps it secret.
Player chooses x_t in[0,1] before target revelation.
Target revealed; player pays(x_t-y_t)^2.
Targets are iid from a fixed distribution on[0,1] chosen at the beginning.
Knowing the distribution permits predicting its mean each round at expected cost sigma²T, with sigma² its variance.
We cannot do better than that.
Distribution is unknown, so compare the strategy to the optimal one.
Cumulative expected excess, equation(1.1).
Equivalently, consider the average.
Average expected excess, equation(1.2).
Both expected excess quantities are nonnegative.
Successful means(1.1) sublinear, equivalently(1.2) tends to0 as T tends to infinity.
Average performance over rounds should approach optimal performance.
Minimizing Regret. Having arrived at a good measure of success...
Rewrite(1.1) equivalently using expected fixed-comparator minimum.
Expected cumulative learner loss minus minimum expected cumulative fixed-action loss.
Remove the data-generation assumption and consider arbitrary sequences y_t.
If the algorithm is deterministic, remove expectation because no stochasticity remains.
Deterministic squared-loss best-fixed regret.
Winning is sublinear regret; best single choice in hindsight defines the comparator meaning.
In iid case a single best prediction is optimal; for arbitrary sequences other comparator sequences could be considered, but a single comparator is chosen for this book's main exposition.
Vector prediction x_t in feasible V subset R^d; loss ell_t:V→R; arbitrary fixed comparator u inV.
Comparator-parameterized regret.
Algorithm need not know u or corresponding regret to guarantee an upper bound.
No-regret is at-most-sublinear regret for every fixed u; printed ordinary-limit inequality.
Remark1.1: regret also depends on losses ell_1,...,ell_T; suppress this dependence.
Footnote1: some settings permit predictions in larger W superset V.

nodes.statement: The pages omit probability-space, measurability and integrability details needed to interpret expectations and random adaptive predictions. Unit-interval laws supply bounded-moment intuition, not a printed measure-theoretic proof.

No proof is printed that the population mean is in the action interval, attains the minimum of expected fixed-action cumulative loss, and has value T sigma^2. The expected-fixed minimum must be attained; no expectation/minimum interchange is licensed.

The assertion that no strategy beats the variance and the subsequent nonnegativity assertion have no printed argument. The missing bridge must account for prediction before revelation, dependence on past observations, and the randomization model if one is added. Mere target IID does not make an arbitrary random prediction independent of the current target.

The finite positive-horizon division identity and the equivalence of sublinear cumulative excess with average excess tending to zero are asserted, without an explicit proof. A finite lower bound alone supplies no successful strategy or convergence.

The contextual pathwise squared-loss minimum is written without an attainment argument. It is a different object from minimum expected fixed loss; it is used already in the definition display, not only its later interpretation.
